entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 8 Jud 8:1-9 . The Ephraimites Offended, but Pacified.
1. the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus?-- Where this complaint was made, whether before or after the crossing of the Jordan, cannot be determined. By the overthrow of the national enemy, the Ephraimites were benefited as largely as any of the other neighboring tribes. But, piqued at not having been sharers in the glory of the victory, their leading men could not repress their wounded pride; and the occasion only served to bring out an old and deep-seated feeling of jealous rivalry that subsisted between the tribes ( Is 9:21 ). The discontent was groundless, for Gideon acted according to divine directions. Besides, as their tribe was conterminous with that of Gideon, they might, had they been really fired with the flame of patriotic zeal, have volunteered their services in a movement against the common enemy.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2299"/><div sID="gen3099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2299"/><hi type="bold">6. the princes of Succoth said, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand--</hi>an insolent as well as a time-serving reply. It was insolent because it implied a bitter taunt that Gideon was counting with confidence on a victory which they believed he would not gain; and it was time-serving, because living in the near neighborhood of the Midianite sheiks, they dreaded the future vengeance of those roving chiefs. This contumelious manner of acting was heartless and disgraceful in people who were of Israelitish blood. <div eID="gen3099" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2315"/><div sID="gen3118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2315"/><hi type="bold">27. Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, ... Ophrah--</hi>That no idolatrous use was in view, nor any divisive course from Shiloh contemplated, is manifest from <reference osisRef="Judg.8.33">Jud 8:33</reference>. Gideon proposed, with the gold he received, to make an ephod for his use only as a civil magistrate or ruler, as David did (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.27">1Ch 15:27</reference>), and a magnificent pectoral or breastplate also. It would seem, from the history, that he was not blamable in making this ephod, as a civil robe or ornament merely, but that it afterward became an object to which religious ideas were attached; whereby it proved a snare, and consequently an evil, by perversion, to Gideon and his house [Taylor, Fragments]. <div eID="gen3118" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 27. Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, ... Ophrah-- That no idolatrous use was in view, nor any divisive course from Shiloh contemplated, is manifest from Jud 8:33 . Gideon proposed, with the gold he received, to make an ephod for his use only as a civil magistrate or ruler, as David did ( 1Ch 15:27 ), and a magnificent pectoral or breastplate also. It would seem, from the history, that he was not blamable in making this ephod, as a civil robe or ornament merely, but that it afterward became an object to which religious ideas were attached; whereby it proved a snare, and consequently an evil, by perversion, to Gideon and his house [Taylor, Fragments].
